title: Are You One of Us? A Qualitative Study of How White Appearing College Students Make Sense of Their Identities, Find Communities, and Interact with Racial and Ethnic Affinity Spaces
abstract: College students of color experience greater harassment and perceive campus climate as more racist and less accepting than their white peers. Racial and ethnic affinity groups aim to provide supports for students of color, but in fact often don’t serve phenotypically ambiguous students. While past research has typically characterized multiracial participants as ambiguous, limited work exists on the identity development and group membership of both monoracial and multiracial white appearing individuals. Even less work focuses on the college context. To address this gap, the present study examines how 10 white appearing college students make sense of their identities and how that understanding informs their experiences finding communities and interacting with racial and ethnic affinity spaces. Using grounded theory to analyze the data from in-person, semi-structured interviews, this study found that white appearing students are often uncertain about their identity and are mainly constructing their racial and ethnic identity via primary caregivers and communities. When seeking communities, they long for acceptance, using their life experiences and performing in ways to justify that their white appearance does not match how they feel. Still, they are rejected by racial and ethnic communities for not being authentic enough. This rejection causes participants to diminish their whiteness and idealize the experiences of people of color as they desire to feel accepted for who they are. Ultimately, most participants leave racial and ethnic communities, finding non-exclusive communities to be more accepting and supportive. These data bring light to how white appearing college students find supports.
